title: What is Node.js?
summary: Explains what a web framework is, why Node.js is a JavaScript runtime rather than a framework, what 'asynchronous and event-driven' means, and why the course picks Node for the backend.

concepts.heading: Framework vs runtime
points: A web framework is a set of ready-made components and structures for building an app, so common plumbing doesn't have to be hand-written every time (illustrated with store-bought vs home-made mayonnaise).
Node.js is not itself a framework. Its own docs describe it as an asynchronous, event-driven JavaScript runtime for building scalable network applications.
A runtime environment is what lets code execute somewhere. JavaScript was originally created only to run inside browsers, so on its own it could not be used for non-website programs.
Node takes Google's V8 engine (from Chromium, written in C/C++, the engine that powers Chrome) and runs it outside the browser, so JavaScript can run directly on any machine: a laptop or a server.
Result: JavaScript can now do the jobs of server-side languages such as Python, Ruby, PHP or C#, including desktop and server-side applications.

concepts.heading: Synchronous vs asynchronous, event-driven
points: Synchronous code (all the scripts written so far) runs top to bottom; each step waits for the previous one to finish, holding resources until it does.
Analogy: ordering a parcel online and being unable to do anything until it arrives would be the synchronous version.

Asynchronous code starts a slow task (file read, network call, database query) and moves on instead of waiting. The follow-up code is packaged as a handler for an event and runs only when that event fires (the 'parcel arrives').
This non-blocking model is why Node is fast and efficient for servers that handle many requests at once.
(Extra) In code this shows up as callback functions, Promises and async/await, which appear in the next lessons (e.g. fs.writeFile's callback).

concepts.heading: Where Node fits in the backend
points: The backend is server + application + database. The server is just a computer with no browser, so something has to run the application code: Node does that for JavaScript.
Node lets you build the application part of the backend in JavaScript on that server.

concepts.heading: Why the course chooses Node
points: One language across the whole stack: HTML/CSS/JS on the frontend and JS on the backend. Easier for frontend devs to move to backend, and code can be shared between client and server.
Scales well for large professional projects.
Fast and non-blocking thanks to the async, event-driven design.
Huge ecosystem: thousands of open-source packages on NPM, plus plenty of docs, tutorials and Stack Overflow answers.
Used in production by companies such as LinkedIn, Twitter, Netflix and NASA.

Node is a key skill employers look for. Python backends (Flask) are a good fit for ML/AI work; PHP and Ruby on Rails are presented as outdated choices for a new bootcamp curriculum. GitHub language stats show JavaScript still at the top.

pitfalls: Calling Node a framework or a language: it is a runtime that executes JavaScript outside the browser (Express, covered later, is the framework).
Assuming code always runs in the order written: with async APIs, the callback runs after the lines that follow it.

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 's23-what-is-node' (blurb: Node runs JavaScript outside the browser using Chrome's V8 engine, and handles slow work asynchronously).
Task 1: sort a list of statements into 'runs in the browser only', 'runs in Node only', 'both' (e.g. document.querySelector, require('fs'), console.log, Math.random).
Task 2: predict the output order of a snippet mixing console.log with setTimeout(..., 0) and a fake readFile callback, then run it in the sandbox to check.
Task 3: label the three parts of a backend (server, application, database) and mark which one Node runs.

Interactive demo idea: a 'synchronous vs asynchronous kitchen' timeline where the learner clicks to start three slow tasks; in sync mode they stack end to end, in async mode they overlap and their callbacks fire as each finishes.
